title: Lake County Wells: Depth, Yield and Drilling Cost
meta_description: Lake County wells have a 106 ft median depth and 10 gpm median yield. See local drilling costs, water-level records and risks before buying land.
h1: What to Expect From a Well in Lake County
intro_html:
A Lake County well budget starts with mountain bedrock, not just a countywide average. The recorded median depth is 106 feet, but the middle half runs from 60 to 165 feet. That spread matters when pricing a lot or comparing drilling bids.

Colorado DWR records contain 2,719 permitted wells countywide, with 1,675 recorded as constructed. For property around Leadville or Leadville North, use these figures as a starting point, then check nearby well logs, the actual permit and the site's access conditions.

sections.heading: Lake County Depths Depend on the Fractures
sections.html:
Among the 1,764 wells reporting depth, the median is 106 feet. The middle half spans 60–165 feet, so a bid based only on the median leaves meaningful room for a deeper hole. The 90th-percentile depth is 290 feet, and the deepest reported well reaches 1,892 feet. That extreme is not a sensible default for a household budget.

Most permits fall in the unnamed or fractured-bedrock category: 2,588 wells, compared with 75 labeled Alluvial and 6 labeled Quaternary Alluvium. In fractured granite and gneiss, usable water depends on the fractures the borehole intersects. A nearby successful well is useful evidence, but it does not guarantee the same depth on your parcel.

sections.heading: A Recorded 10 gpm Is Encouraging, Not a Guarantee
sections.html:
The 739 wells with reported pump yields have a 10.0 gpm median, with the middle half at 6.0–12.0 gpm. The largest share, 74%, reports 5–15 gpm. Those results are encouraging for household supply, but a recorded yield describes a test result, not a promise of continuous output under every condition.

At the lower end, 12% report 1–5 gpm and 1% report under 1 gpm. A low-producing well can require storage and careful demand management. Before buying, have the existing well's pumping performance and recovery evaluated. Also check authorized use: a well's physical capacity does not establish permission for livestock, irrigation or other outdoor demands.

sections.heading: Lake County Water Levels Do Not Show a Clear Decline
sections.html:
Static water level means the depth to standing water when the well is not being pumped. Only 223 wells report that measurement. Their median is 93 feet below ground, and the middle half is 52–172 feet. These are different records from the full depth dataset; subtracting the county medians will not tell you how much water an individual well stores.

The decade medians are 115 feet below surface in the 2010s and 90 feet in the 2020s. The later figure is shallower, so this series does not demonstrate a dropping water table. It also does not prove countywide recovery: different wells, locations and measurement conditions can change the median. Seek repeat measurements from the property itself.

sections.heading: Who Drilled Lake County's Recorded Wells
sections.html:
Permit activity was strongest in the supplied decade totals during the 1990s, with 516 permits, followed by 502 in the 2000s. Records show 276 in the 2010s and 234 in the 2020s, with the newest permit dated 2025. The later decade is incomplete, so it is not a clean comparison of long-term demand.

The most active recorded drillers are Golden Eagle Drilling Corporation (Shelton, Joe Wayne) with 685 wells, Twin Lakes Drilling Co. (Schaffer, James O) with 204, and Steve Shelton Drilling, Inc. (Shelton, Steve) with 122. These are historical record counts, not confirmation of current availability. Domestic/household use accounts for 81% of permits, while monitoring accounts for 10%; not every mapped well represents a residential supply.

sections.heading: Budgeting a New Well Near Leadville
sections.html:
The Lake County cost model assumes fractured mountain bedrock and a drilling rate of $65–$100 per foot. At the 106-foot median depth, the drilled hole is approximately $6,900–$10,600. A finished well with pump, tank, trenching and electrical is modeled at $12,900–$22,600. Treat that as a planning range, not a parcel-specific quote.

The 60–165-foot middle depth range explains why bids should state how added footage is charged. Ask what casing, grout, testing and completion work are included, and what happens if the initial hole produces poorly. Around Leadville and Leadville North, review rig access and the route to the proposed home before accepting a price. A short borehole does not automatically mean a simple finished installation.

sections.heading: Mine History and Water Quality Need a Parcel-Level Check
sections.html:
The environmental mapping identifies 4,731 historic mine features, 21 EPA Superfund/cleanup sites and 22 PFAS sampling/contamination sites within about 10 miles. Those counts are reasons to investigate location and groundwater context, not proof that a particular household well is contaminated. A PFAS sampling location does not, by itself, establish a contaminated result.

Have a qualified laboratory test the water and ask local health officials which additional analyses fit the property's mine and cleanup-site setting. Review casing, grout and wellhead condition as well. The 1% share reporting under 1 gpm describes low reported production, not the chance of a dry hole. For a buildable lot, confirm that the well, septic system and home can meet applicable siting requirements before finalizing the layout.

sections.heading: Before Closing on a Lake County Well Property
sections.html:
Start with the parcel's DWR permit, construction report and any pump-test or laboratory records. Confirm that the permitted uses match your plans; an exempt household-use well may not authorize the outdoor uses a buyer expects. An existing well on a map is not enough to establish a usable, legally suitable water supply.

Compare neighboring logs around Leadville or Leadville North before relying on a broader regional example. Summit County is 26 miles away and Chaffee County is 36 miles away, but distance alone does not make their wells good comparisons in mountain terrain. For vacant land, coordinate drilling access, septic feasibility and the home layout early. For an existing home, make water quality and demonstrated well performance part of purchase due diligence.

faq.q: How deep are wells in Lake County, Colorado?
faq.a: The recorded median depth is 106 feet, and the middle half of wells is 60–165 feet deep. The 90th-percentile depth is 290 feet. Lake County's fractured mountain bedrock makes parcel-level results unpredictable, so compare nearby construction logs and ask how a drilling bid handles added footage rather than budgeting only for the median.

faq.q: How much does it cost to drill a well in Lake County?
faq.a: The local model uses $65–$100 per foot for fractured mountain bedrock. At the 106-foot median depth, the drilled hole is about $6,900–$10,600. A finished well with pump, tank, trenching and electrical is about $12,900–$22,600. Get a written scope covering casing, grout, access and completion work before treating that range as your project budget.

faq.q: How much water do Lake County wells produce?
faq.a: Among 739 wells with reported pump yields, the median is 10.0 gpm and the middle half is 6.0–12.0 gpm. Reported yields under 1 gpm account for 1%. These records help set expectations, but an existing property's pumping performance and recovery need evaluation before you depend on it for household supply.

faq.q: Is well water safe to drink in Lake County?
faq.a: Safety cannot be determined from a permit or county averages. Mapping identifies 4,731 historic mine features, 21 EPA Superfund/cleanup sites and 22 PFAS sampling/contamination sites within about 10 miles; proximity does not establish contamination in your well. Obtain laboratory testing and ask local health officials which analyses fit the property's setting and nearby environmental history.

faq.q: Is the water table dropping in Lake County?
faq.a: The available decade medians do not show a decline: reported static water levels were 115 feet below ground in the 2010s and 90 feet in the 2020s. Shallower water is not evidence of a falling table. However, only 223 wells report static levels, and changing measurement locations prevent treating these medians as proof of countywide recovery.
